title: Participle clauses with adverbial meaning 2
subtitle: By working hard, ... / Without meaning to, ...
summary: Use preposition + -ing clauses, by / in / on + -ing, with and without + -ing, and verbless clauses after a conjunction or adjective.

lesson.heading: preposition + -ing
lesson.text: Prepositions such as after, before, besides, by, in, on, since, through, while, with and without can introduce an -ing clause with an adverbial meaning. The passive form is being + past participle.

examples.text: **While understanding** her problem, I don't know how I can help.
**After spending** so much money on the car, I can't afford a holiday.
**Before being changed** last year, the speed limit was 70 kph.

lesson.note: A full clause is the less formal alternative: Since moving to London, we haven't had time to go to the theatre. / Since we moved to London, ...

lesson.heading: by, in, on + -ing
rows: **By working** hard, she passed her maths exam. / They only survived **by eating** roots and berries in the forest.
**On returning** from Beijing, he wrote to the Chinese embassy. / Josh was the first person I saw **on leaving** hospital.
the cause, or the consequence of the action
**In criticising** the painting, I knew I would offend her. / **In choosing** Marco, the People's Party has moved to the left.

lesson.heading: by or in?
lesson.text: by + -ing and in + -ing often overlap, with by preferred in informal contexts. But when the focus is clearly the method, only by is possible.

examples.text: **In** / **By writing** about Spanish culture, I came to understand the country better.
examples.note: In writing ... = the consequence; By writing ... = the method I used

examples.text: **By telephoning** every hour, she managed to speak to the doctor.

lesson.heading: with + -ing for a reason
lesson.text: with + subject + -ing introduces a reason for the main clause. This use is fairly informal, and a subject has to come between with and the -ing form. with and what with can also introduce a reason with a plain noun phrase.

examples.text: **With Louise living** in Spain, we don't see her often.
**With my bad back** I won't be able to lift a heavy suitcase.
**What with** the traffic and the heavy rain, it's no wonder you were late.

lesson.heading: without + -ing
lesson.text: without + -ing says that a second action does not happen. It often also has the meaning 'although ... not' or 'unless'.

examples.text: I went to work **without eating** breakfast.
**Without meaning** to, I seem to have offended her.
**Without using** the app, I can't judge how good it is.

lesson.heading: Clauses with no verb at all
lesson.text: In fairly formal English a clause can begin with a conjunction or an adjective and have no verb. It means the same as a clause with conjunction + subject + be.

examples.text: **While in Poland**, they will play two concerts in Warsaw.
examples.note: or While they are in Poland ...

examples.text: **Although just two feet apart**, they didn't speak.
I try to use public transport **whenever possible**.
**Unhappy with the decision**, Johnson swore at the referee.

lesson.text: Ask what the -ing clause answers: 'how?' takes by, 'when?' takes on, and 'with what result?' takes in.

exercises.prompt: ___ the back off the computer, make sure it is unplugged.
exercises.explanation: preposition + -ing replaces a full time clause (before you take ...).

exercises.prompt: ___ Oxford University in 1983, Painter spent three years teaching at a local school.
exercises.explanation: after + -ing for an event that came first.

exercises.prompt: ___ to the public, most milk is pasteurised.
exercises.explanation: The milk is sold by someone else, so we need the passive form being + past participle.

exercises.prompt: ___ on TV last night, the minister mentioned that she would be retiring soon.
exercises.explanation: while + being + past participle: she was the person interviewed.

exercises.prompt: Match each clause with the main clause that follows it.

pairs.right: she found Dave waiting outside her front door.
she soon began to lose weight.
she gave up the possibility of a huge salary.

pairs.left: By moving to a smaller flat,
pairs.right: she saved over a hundred pounds a month.
she was surprised when all the children stood up.
she knew that she might offend him.

exercises.prompt: ___ every hour, she managed to speak to the doctor.
exercises.explanation: The method is the focus here, not the consequence, so only by + -ing works.

exercises.prompt: ___ having flu, we couldn't go on holiday.
exercises.explanation: with + subject + -ing gives the reason; the subject must come between with and the -ing form.

exercises.prompt: ___ it, he had solved the problem.
exercises.explanation: Here without + -ing means 'although he didn't realise it'.

exercises.prompt: Reduce the opening clause: When she was asked what the secret of her success was, she said, 'Just hard work and a little luck.'
options: When asked what the secret of her success was, she said ...
When asking what the secret of her success was, she said ...
When to ask what the secret of her success was, she said ...
exercises.explanation: The verb was passive, so the reduced clause keeps the past participle: When asked ...

exercises.statement: I try to use public transport whenever possible.
exercises.explanation: Correct. A verbless clause after a conjunction (= whenever it is possible) is normal in fairly formal English.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite with With ... -ing: I couldn't wait for Andrei any longer as time was running out before the train left.
exercises.answer: With time running out before the train left, I couldn't wait for Andrei any longer.

exercises.prompt: Reduce and reorder: She is determined to continue her research and she has recently begun work on her PhD.
exercises.answer: Determined to continue her research, she has recently begun work on her PhD.
exercises.explanation: An adjective can open a verbless clause (= Because she is determined ...).
